en: Now follow the fire-altar constructions (*agnicaya*). We shall explain their measurements and layouts on the ground.

Now, regarding the measurement of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*): fourteen atoms (*aṇu*), thirty-four broad and closely joined sesame seeds—this is another [definition]. Ten *aṅgulas* make a small step (*kṣudrapada*). Twelve [aṅgulas] make a span (*prādeśa*). In the "wider subsequent pair" (*pṛthottarayuga*) system, thirteen [aṅgulas] make a step (*pada*). One hundred and eighty-eight [aṅgulas] make a pole (*īṣā*). Four hundred [aṅgulas] make an axle (*akṣa*). Eighty-six [aṅgulas] make a yoke (*yuga*). Thirty-two [aṅgulas] make a knee (*jānu*). Thirty-six [aṅgulas] make a *śamyā*-arm (*śamyābāhu*). Two steps make a stride (*prakrama*). Two spans make a cubit (*aratni*).

Moreover, they cite this: "In matters of measurement—whether it be a *pada*, a *yuga*, a *prakrama*, an *aratni*, an *iyati*, or a *śamyā*—one may proceed according to one's desire. A man is five *aratnis* in height, as is a *vyāma*. A *vyāyāma* is four *aratnis*.

One desiring to make a square should take a cord of the desired length, fasten loops at both ends, and make a mark in the middle. Having drawn a line, one should drive a peg into its center. Having fastened the two loops to that peg, one should trace a circle with the mark. One should drive pegs at the two ends of the diameter. Having fastened a loop to the eastern peg, one should trace a circle with the loop. Likewise on the western peg; where those two circles meet, from there one should stretch a second diameter.

One should drive stakes at the two ends of the *viṣkambha*. Having fastened the two loops on the eastern side, one should trace a circle with a marking-line. Likewise on the south, likewise on the west, and likewise on the north; that which is the junction of their outermost points becomes a square. 4.

Now, another method: having made a cord twice the measure [of the side] with loops at both ends, he makes a mark in the middle; that serves for the eastern shoulder. On the other half, he makes a mark one-fourth part from the end; that is the "lowering" (nyañcana). Half [the cord] is for the shoulder. Having fastened the two loops at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he should draw out the hips and shoulders by means of the "lowering" and the southern half [of the cord]. 5

One desiring to make a long rectangle should drive two stakes into as much ground as he intends to measure; [he should place] two [stakes] on each side, equidistant from one another. Having made a cord of the same length as the transverse measurement with loops at both ends, he makes a mark in the middle. Having fastened the two loops to the last two of the eastern stakes, he pulls it southward by means of the mark and makes a mark upon the mark.
Having fastened two middle loops, having pulled [the cord] southward over the mark, one should drive a peg into the mark. By this, the northern shoulder is explained; likewise the two hips.
Where one would measure a shorter distance in front, there one makes a mark at half of that.

Now, another method: having made a cord one and a half times the measurement with loops at both ends, he makes a mark on the third part from the other end, which is the sixth part [of the whole]. That is the "downward-mark" (nyañchana). It is for the purpose of determining the shoulders. Having fastened the two loops at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he should draw out the hips and shoulders by moving southward along the downward-mark and using the measured distance as the shoulder-measure. 9. The diagonal cord of a square of equal sides produces an area twice as large. 10. The cross-measuring cord (*tiryak-dvikaraṇī*) is the side-measurement; its diagonal cord is the triple-measuring cord (*trikaraṇī*).

By this, the third operation is explained; as for the ninth, it is that which becomes a part of the ground. 11. The diagonal cord of a long rectangle produces both that which the side-measuring cord and the cross-measuring cord produce when they are separate. 12. The attainment [of the area] occurs in these cases: in those of the triad and tetrad, the twelve and the five, the fifteen and the eight, the seven and the twenty-four, the twelve and the thirty-five, and the fifteen and the thirty-six. 13.

On a square of various dimensions, one should mark out the diagonal of the larger [square] by means of the side-measure of the smaller. The cord drawn diagonally across the diagonal becomes the side-measure for both combined squares. When one wishes to subtract a square from a square, one should mark out the diagonal of the larger [square] by means of the side-measure of the [smaller] square one intends to subtract. One should bring the other side of the diagonal up against the side-measure of the diagonal. Where that [cord] falls, there one should cut it off. By means of what is cut off, the excess is removed.

One who wishes to make a square equal [in area] to a long rectangle should cut off a diagonal portion from it, divide that part into two, and place them on the two sides as appropriate. Alternatively, having made a square within that [long rectangle], one should cut off a side-measure (karaṇī) from it; what remains should be placed upon the other [portion]. One who wishes to make a long rectangle equal [in area] to a square should make the transverse measure (tiryaṅmānī) the side-measure (karaṇī), divide the remainder into two, and place them on the two sides. One should fill up the deficiency by adding small pieces (khaṇḍa). The method for removing such a deficiency has been stated.

Desiring to make one side of a quadrangle narrow, one should make the diagonal measuring-line of the narrow side its cross-measuring-line; having divided the remainder diagonally, one should transpose it and place it on the other side. (6) Desiring to make a quadrangular *prauga* altar, one should make a square ground twice as large as the area desired; having made it a regular square, one should drive a peg into the middle of the eastern measuring-line. Having fastened two loops to that peg, one should drop them onto the southern and northern corners (*śroṇī*). One should cut off the excess cord outside. (7)

One who wishes to make a *prauga* (a rectangular altar with two corners protruding) on both sides should first make a long rectangle as large as he desires. Having done so, he should drive a peg into the middle of the eastern side-line. Having fastened two loops to that peg, he should drop them at the midpoints of the southern and northern sides. He should cut away the cord outside [the desired shape]. By this, the other *prauga* is explained. One who wishes to make a circle out of a square should draw a diagonal line from the center toward the east. What remains beyond that line, one-third of it together with the whole, should be used to trace the circle.

One desiring to make a square mandala should divide the diameter into eight parts, then subdivide one part into twenty-nine parts, and remove twenty-eight of those parts, as well as the sixth part of a part minus one-eighth. Alternatively, having divided [the diameter] into fifteen parts, one should remove two. This is the standard method for making a square. One should increase the measurement by a third, and that [third] by a fourth diminished by one-thirty-fourth; this is the specific rule.

Now, regarding the sacrificial enclosure for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*): the location of the *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya* is prescribed as follows: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish his fire at eight steps, a Rājanya at eleven, and a Vaiśya at twelve.

One should have three squares made, each measuring one-third of the length, arranged consecutively. The *gārhapatya* is at the northern corner of the western [square]. The *anvāhāryapacana* is on its southern shoulder; the *āhavanīya* is on the northern shoulder of the eastern [square].

Alternatively, having divided the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires into five or six parts, and having added an additional sixth or seventh part to make them equal, he divides it into three equal portions. He makes a mark at the end of two of these portions from the eastern end. Having fixed the two ends of the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya, he draws a line toward the south using the mark as a guide and drives a peg into that mark; this becomes the location for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. 3.

Alternatively, one may increase the measurement by a fifth part. Having divided that entire length into five parts, one makes a mark at two points from the opposite end. Having fastened the two loops at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord, one pulls it southward along the mark and drives a peg into the mark; this becomes the location for the *dakṣiṇāgni*. By reversing this procedure, the *utkara* is explained.
"The *āhavanīya* is to the west [of the *dakṣiṇāgni*] and is measured to the height of the sacrificer"—this is known from the altar of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Its transverse side at the back is three parts less than that; its transverse side in front is half of that very [side]. Having thus divided the long quadrangle so as to be narrow on one side, one should drive stakes into the corners. 7.

Having made a cord twice as long as the side-measure and having provided loops at both ends, he makes a mark in the middle. Having fastened the two loops on the two southern sides and having pulled [the cord] southward by means of the mark, he should drive a peg into the mark. Having fastened the two loops onto that peg, he should trace around the southern side by means of the mark. By this, the northern side is explained. He should trace around the eastern side with that [cord] doubled; likewise the western [side]. 8.

"It is ten steps long from west to east, twelve steps wide from south to north, and eight steps long from east to west"—thus is the altar for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) known. Its measurement has been explained. According to some, it is equal to a chariot; according to others, it is equal to a *virāj* [verse].
"It is four-cornered and the size of a yoke-pin (*śamyā*)"—thus is the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) known. It is a perfect square, as there is no distinction [stated otherwise].

"The altar is one-third [of the Mahāvedi]," so it is understood from the *Paitṛka* altar. It becomes the third side-measure (*karaṇī*) of the Mahāvedi when it has been made into a square. However, let there be a ninth part of the ground. According to some, it is four-cornered and measured by the sacrificer's own height; its corners are situated in the cardinal directions. 11.

Regarding the third [measurement], they prescribe the Sautrāmaṇī altar according to the rule "one should sacrifice on the third. Of the Mahāvedi, which has been made a perfect square, the side-measure is eighteen *pada*s. Regarding its lengthening and the making of it narrow on one side, one may act as one desires.
12. The *prāgvamśa* (fore-hall) is sixteen *prakrama*s in length and twelve in width; or else, it is twelve *prakrama*s in length and ten in width. 1.
In the middle of that is the twelve-cubit sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). 2.

It is known from the *Mahāvedi* [text] that it has thirty paces or steps as its transverse side toward the west, thirty-six toward the east, and twenty-four as its transverse side toward the north. The method of measuring it has been explained. Six paces from the *Āhavanīya* fire is the *Mahāvedi*. In one of those [six], there is the *Sadas*; that is ten [paces]. To the north, it is twenty-seven *aratnis*; according to some, eighteen. Then, in four [of those], there is the *Havirdhāna* shed; that is ten or twelve [paces]. The method of measuring those two has been explained.

Leaving half a *prakrama* from the peg at the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭīya*), he measures out the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). It is known from the *Soma* ritual that the northern altar consists of ten paces; its method of measurement has been explained. (6) The *cātvāla* pit is either the measure of a *śamyā* or of unlimited size. (7) Now, the *uparava* holes have openings of one span (*prādeśa*) and intervals of one span. Having marked out a square of one cubit (*aratni*) on all sides, one should drive pegs into the corners. With an interval of half a span each, one should draw a circle around each individual [corner]. (8)

Leaving a space of two steps from the eastern half of the *sadas*, the diameter of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths and their intervals are each two *prādeśas*. (9) The side-measure of the *āgnīdhra* shed is five *aratnis*.
(10) By this, the *mārjālīya* shed is explained. They make its door face north. (11)

"It is known from the *Ekādaśinī* sacrifice that the sacrificial post-holes are at the distance of a chariot-axle. One should take a twenty-fourth part of ten chariot-axles, eleven foot-steps, and eight finger-breadths; that shall be the *prakrama*. With that he measures out the altar. (12) "Now, in the *Aśvamedha*, one should take a twenty-fourth part of twenty chariot-axles, twenty-one foot-steps, and eight finger-breadths; that shall be the *prakrama*. With that he measures out the altar. (13)

Now, from the eastern half of the altar, one should cut off a portion measuring half a *pada* for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) belonging to the eastern set of eleven posts, and place it to the east, facing forward. In this case, the eight-finger measurement does not apply, nor is there any interlocking.
(Sūtra 14) The sacrificial post-holes have a width of one *pada*, and the tops of the posts have a circumference of three *padas*.

(Sūtra 15) The first fire-altar consists of seven and a half men's lengths; the second, eight and a half; the third, nine and a half. In this manner, the successive increase in the number of parts continues up to the one-hundred-and-one-fold altar. Thus, this [system of fire-altars] begins with the sevenfold and ends with the one-hundred-and-one-fold. (Sūtra 1)

From this point forward, one should undertake only those sacrifices consisting of one hundred and one forms; or else, one may perform sacrificial rites that do not require the sacred fires, with the exception of the Aśvamedha.

If one should undertake the Aśvamedha before reaching its proper time, one should practice the prescribed forms from this point onward and disregard the rest. If one should undertake it prematurely, having undertaken it, one should resume from the very point where it was left off.
How, indeed, should one practice the *vidhā*?

Whatever is other than the *prakṛti*, having divided that into fifteen parts, one should combine two parts for each *vidhā*. With those [parts], numbering seven and a half, one should pile the fire-altar. Some hand down the rule that the practice of the vertical measurement should be done with the twenty-fourth part of the fifth [section] of the knee.
Now, some indeed construct [the altar] with one kind [of brick] and so forth, without wings and tail;
that is not tenable, because of the contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Now, for some there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "The first layer of the fires is that of the Śyena."

Now, as for others [who say]: "Having piled a larger [altar], one should not pile a smaller one"—this is our position. It has wings; for that which is wingless cannot fly. The two wings are longer by one *aratni*. Therefore, birds have wings for flight. The wings and the tail are each a fathom (*vyāma*) in measure. There is no eagle found without wings and tail, nor do wings and tail exist for one who has not piled the sevenfold [altar]. Nor does the piling of the sevenfold lead to the contingency of the single-fold. Therefore, the first fire-altar is indeed sevenfold.

One should avoid the *bheda* (divisions). They teach that *bheda* refers to the joining of the sides of the lower and upper [layers]. That is not found at the ends of the fire-altars, nor at the corners or the sides.
"One should pile the thousand-brick altar when piling for the first time";
or one should complete the count on the fifth layer.

If one should wish to construct [the altar] with two hundred [bricks], one should employ five *coḍā* bricks to correspond to the same number for the *nākasad* bricks. Indeed, Agni has the nature of an animal. Just as in an animal, that which is the right side of the bones on the right side becomes the left side of those on the left, and that which is the left side of those on the left becomes the right side of those on the right; and what is both downward and upward is the same—so too should one lay down the forms of the bricks.

Those lines which turn to the right, he should place on the south; those which turn to the left, on the north. There are straight lines behind and in front; in the middle, they are triple-lined. Now, as for those which are interlacing: just as the backbone of an animal does not run along one side exclusively nor along the other, so should one understand the laying down of those [bricks]. Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Prajāpati indeed is Atharvan; Agni is Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; his bricks are the bones."
Therefore, if one should pile up [bricks] outside the body, one should join them from the middle of the destruction of the body to the middle of the destruction of the self.
"One piles this facing east," so it is known.
One should not complete the count with non-clay bricks that are not *iṣṭakās*.
"From this Brāhmaṇa passage: 'One fire-altar consists of piled bricks, while another consists of animals';
and also: 'This Agni is indeed an animal; truly, that part of the animal which is fashioned prior to the brick-laying is performed as the Yajus-verse.
(7) One should place materials that obstruct the [visible] world into the pits. (9)
One should recognize the marks on the bricks with the formulas: "The mandala," "the bull," and "Vikarṇī.

(10) Since there is no fixed measure [for the number of bricks], the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are employed when the two brick-formulas are not otherwise applicable. (11) One should place here only those groups of bricks that have already been mentioned. (12)
There are five world-filling [bricks].
(13) One should place pebbles mentioned apart from the mantras at the joints.
(14) "He places them facing east," "he places them facing west"—such is the statement regarding the *rīti* (alignment) within the groups. (15)
"He lays down one facing east, he lays down one facing west"—this is a figurative expression regarding the agent's orientation. 16.
"He lays down others in the east facing west, and others in the west facing east"—this refers to the completion of the work. 17.
This is applicable only to those bricks that are square. 18.

One should not lay down a broken brick; one should not lay down a shattered brick; one should not lay down a black brick; one should not lay down a decayed brick; one should not lay down a marked brick; nor should one lay down a *svayamātṛṇṇā* (naturally perforated) brick upon a self-piled altar.
The vertical measurement of the bricks should be made with the fifth part of the knee; for the *nākasad* bricks and the five *coḍā* bricks, it should be half [of that].
Whatever may be deficient due to drying or baking, one should fill that up with *purīṣa* (clay soil), since there is no fixed measure for the *purīṣa*.
"It becomes the measure of physical exertion," so it is known from the Gārhapatya altar.
According to some, it is square; according to others, it is circular.
Having divided the square into seven parts, one should divide it transversely into three parts. In the subsequent layer, one lays down the bricks facing north.

If one were to lay down [the bricks] as perfect squares, one should have the bricks made with the sixth part of a vyāyāma, or with the fourth or the third part. Of these, nine are first [in size] and twelve are second; one lays them down in the first layer. Five are third [in size] and sixteen are first; one lays them down in the subsequent [layer].

Having made a circular area as square as possible, one should divide it into nine parts, and the *pradhīs* into three by three. One should lay down the subsequent layer in such a way that the corners fall upon the faces of the *pradhīs*.
The hearths (dhiṣṇyas) are single-layered, either square or circular.

9. Having divided the Āgnīdhrīya hearth into nine parts, one should place a stone in the place of one of those parts. 10. Then, having divided the Hotṛ’s hearth into nine parts, one should divide each of the three front parts into two. 11.
Then, having divided the other [space] ninefold and ninefold, one should combine the two parts—the middle and the front—into one. 12.
Then, having divided the *mārjālīya* hearth threefold, one should divide the front and rear portions fivefold. 13.
Having mixed them with the ashes from the *ukhya* fire-pot, one should have bricks made. 14.
This applies to one who has maintained the fire for a year, not to one who has maintained it for only a night;
thus is his construction of the altar accompanied by mantras.
One may construct the *chandaścita* altar beyond the three-thousand-fold [altar] according to one's specific desire; its form is that of a hawk.
Now, it is indeed said: "One desiring heaven should pile the Śyenacit.
There are two types of forms: the square-shaped body and the falcon-shaped form. Both are known from the Brāhmaṇa.

He places five [bricks] on the southern hip and five on the northern hip. He places [a brick] on the southern shoulder with the formula, "The ram is the age," and on the northern [shoulder] with, "The bull is the age. He places [a brick] on the southern wing with, "The tiger is the age," and on the northern [wing] with, "The lion is the age. And [he places one] in the middle with, "Man is the age. Now, furthermore, this Agni is built as a likeness of the various ages; that is to say, by means of the shadow of those [beings] as they fly upward. He builds the fire-altar with bricks that are equal squares, for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human—so says the Maitrāyaṇīya Brāhmaṇa.
One should have bricks made for it [the altar] with a side equal to the fourth, fifth, sixth, or tenth part of a man.
Now he measures out the fire-altar:

as long as a man is with his arms raised, so long he makes two openings in the bamboo pole at the interval; the third [mark] is in the middle. What he does there with a cord, he does here with the bamboo pole.

Its body is a square of four *puruṣas*. Each wing is a square of one *puruṣa*, but it is longer by one *aratni* on the south side. By this, the northern wing is explained. The tail is a square of one *puruṣa*; one should extend it by one *prādeśa* at the bottom. In this way, the sevenfold altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is fully described.

On the *upadhāna* (laying), at the third man’s length to the north of the tip of the wing, one should place four *pañcamī* bricks; on both sides of these, two *pāda*-bricks each; then eight *caturthī* bricks. One should cover the remainder of the wing with *ṣaḍbhāgīyā* bricks. By this, the northern wing is explained. 11.

On the front and rear sides of the tail, one should lay *caturbhāgīyā* bricks; on the southern and northern [sides], *pāda*-bricks. One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar (*agni*) with *pañcamabhāgīyā* bricks. 12. This is the two-hundred-brick layer (*prastāra*). 13.

In the subsequent arrangement, one should lay down the bricks in reverse order: three sixty-fingers [bricks] and two two-padas each at the interval of half a vyāyāma to the north of the tip of the wing. Likewise on the north side.

On the southern hip, nine sixty-fingers [bricks] are laid down in square form; likewise on the northern hip, nine ninety-fingers [bricks] and two two-padas each—one should lay them down in reverse order from the southern shoulder to the northern shoulder.

One should cover the remaining fire-altar with bricks measuring five parts. 17 This is the two-hundred-brick layer; one should pile them in alternating fashion for as many layers as one intends to construct. 18 Now, another [method]. 19.

There are five *puruṣa*-length bricks for the male [altar]. These same [bricks] are one and a half [bricks] on one side. Among them, the half-bricks and the quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) are used in the laying. One should lay the half-bricks facing north on the two sides of the wings, in the front and back parts. Likewise, on the northern [side], one should lay four and four one-and-a-half bricks facing north on the two sides of the tail, southern and northern. Below the tail, one should lay four half-bricks facing north. On both sides of these, there are two quarter-bricks. Behind the junctions of the tail, one should lay one half-brick each, facing east.
One should cover the remaining fire-altar with bricks measuring five parts;

this is the two-hundred-brick layering. In the subsequent layering, one should place four quarter-bricks on the side-ridges of the body; around these, there are two half-bricks each. On the front shoulder, there are five.
At the two tips of the wings, one should lay three bricks each, measuring one and a half [units], facing north. In the spaces between them, one should place a single half-brick each, facing east.
One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with bricks consisting of a fifth part.
This is the two-hundred-brick layer; one should pile it in alternating fashion for as many layers as one intends to construct.

Now, [the altar] with curved sides and a split tail: one should have its bricks made from the fourth part of a man's height; half of those are for the *pādya* (foot) bricks and half for the *ārdhya* (half-brick) bricks. When no specific instruction is given, the removal of the *akṣṇya* (corner) bricks is obligatory.

One should enclose the *pādeṣṭakās* (foot-bricks) with four [types]: by a quarter-part, by a full part, by a half-and-a-quarter part, and by a part plus a fraction. One should have the *ardheṣṭakā* (half-brick) made in such a way that two of them would join together lengthwise.

Then he measures out the fire-altar. The body (ātman) is two puruṣas in length and ten paces in width. From its southern shoulder, he makes a mark one and a half prakramas to the north; likewise on the other side. Having stretched a cord over those two marks, he should cut off the shoulder [of the altar]. By this, the cutting off of the other corners is explained. That is the body. The head is one and a half paces in length and half a puruṣa in width. He should cut off its shoulders at intervals of one prakrama each.

The tail has six padas facing east and two puruṣas facing north. One should shorten its eastern corner by three steps each. The wing has a length of twelve padas and a width of ten padas. Having stepped six padas eastward from its middle, one should drive in a peg; likewise, one peg at each of the two hips. Then one should enclose it with a cord. Having cut out the inner part of the cord, one should place it extending eastward in front; that is the "bend" (nirṇāma). By this, the bend of the northern wing is explained.

Having made five squares, each measuring one *prakrama*, aligned lengthwise at the tips of the two wings, one should cut them off diagonally toward the bottom and remove the halves. (8) In this way, the sevenfold altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed. (9) In the laying of the bricks, one should place the fourth brick at the end of the head. A *haṃsamukhī* brick is placed in front. Two *pādeṣṭakā*s are placed on both sides. Below those, three square *pādyā* bricks are placed on each side. The remaining space is filled with *pādeṣṭakā*s. (10)

Alternatively, one should place the Haṃsamukhī brick at the front of the head; below that, one should place the fourth brick on both sides of the two foot-bricks (pādeṣṭakā). Below those, there should be three square foot-bricks on each side. In the remaining space of the foot, one should place five foot-bricks interlaced [with others]. Likewise, in front of the tail, wherever there is a deficiency, one should place half-foot-bricks (ardheṣṭakā) and foot-bricks. One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with quarter-bricks (caturbhāgīyā). One should complete the count with foot-bricks and half-foot-bricks.
This is the two-hundred-brick layout (14).

In the other layout, one should join four *haṃsamukhī* bricks with four *pādeṣṭakā*s so that it results in a long square. One should place that transversely in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick (15).
Two *haṃsamukhī*s facing west are placed at the junction of the tail, with half a brick's width in the body. Below them, on both sides, one should place three *pādeṣṭakā*s facing east (16).
Below the tail, one should lay fifteen foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) interlaced.

(17) One should pile the wing-tiles with the bricks oriented eastward, alternating between foot-bricks and half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*). (18) In the doubtful area, where there is a gap, one should lay half-bricks and foot-bricks. (19)
One should cover the remaining space with four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*). One should complete the count with foot-bricks (*pādyā*) and half-foot-bricks (*sārdhyā*). 20.
Now, another [method]: for a person, by means of fifth-parts, one hundred and eighty-seven and a half [bricks], including the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, result in a sevenfold altar. 2.
Of those [bricks], fifty-two and a half each should be placed on the head; fifteen in the tail; and fifty-eight and a half on the right wing. Likewise on the left.

The cutting away of the corners is by half a vyāyāma. The tail is curved. The bending of the two wings is by three aratnis each. One should make six segments with bricks measuring one and a half [vyāyāmas] each. The shape of the head is constant. Now follow the modifications of the bricks.

Those same five [units] on one side are one and a half; those same [five] on the other side are one and a quarter. There are quarter-units and half-and-a-quarter units of the fifth-part unit; likewise for the one-and-a-half unit. One should join the eighth-parts of those two in such a way that three sides are formed, as well as the eighth-parts of the fifth-part unit. One should place ten fifth-part units, including the half-and-a-quarter ones, in the body; likewise in the tail, and in the two wings, one-and-a-half units including the half-and-a-quarter ones.
Those [bricks] which arise on the head:
in the next layer, one should place one of each of the two types on each of the two ends of the wings; one on each of the two [ends] of the other [wing]; and two on each of the two sides of the head.

Below the tail, one should place bricks measuring one and a half [units] facing east according to the available space; on the two sides, [one should place] the *pādyā* bricks with an eighth part added.
On the two wings, one should lay down twelve bricks with fractional parts and one and a half [bricks];
the remainder should be laid down according to suitability, according to number, and according to the rule.
By this, the body and the tail of the Kaṅkacit are explained.
One should place five [bricks] on the head; its form has been explained. One should place fifty-seven [bricks] on the right wing, and likewise on the left.
The bending of the two wings is by means of the span plus a *prādeśa*. One should make six petals on each side with bricks measuring half of a fifth-part brick. One and a half [bricks] remain over.

Below that tail [of the altar], two feet—one *aratni* in length and separated by an interval of one *aratni*—are each one *prādeśa* in width. Below those, on both sides, one should place two-eighths (one-quarter) each, with their narrow ends facing east.
In this way, the sevenfold altar, together with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed.

Now follow the modifications of the bricks. Those with parts consist of fifth-parts. One should surround a quarter-brick (pādeṣṭakā) with four [parts]: half-a-prādeśa, one and a half prādeśas, one prādeśa, and a prādeśa plus a fraction. One should surround a one-and-a-half brick (adhyardheṣṭakā) with four [parts]: half a vyāyāma, two aratnis, and an aratni plus a fraction. These are six [types]. Of these, having laid down the square quarter-bricks which have an eighth part [added] at the two quarters, one should lay down the remainder as appropriate, according to number, and according to rule.
By this, the head and the tail of the *alaja* altar are explained, having excluded the two feet.
One should lay down sixty-three bricks on the right wing; likewise on the left.
By means of a *puruṣa*, there is the bending away of the two wings.
Having measured one cubit (aratni) eastward from the next backward bend and having fixed a cord there, he should extend another wing-section cut-off.

In this way, five [sections] are removed, each being half of a fifth. Having laid down a quarter-brick at the bend, one should remove from among them the square quarter-bricks that have an eighth part [of a brick] added.

The remainder he should arrange according to what is appropriate, according to number, and according to the rule. 6. "One should pile the *prauga* altar. Having made the *prauga* as large as the fire-altar itself, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, one should have twelve bricks made from its rear diagonal cord, with half that measurement as their width. Of these, some are half-sized and some are quarter-sized. 2.
Of those [bricks], one should place two half-iṣṭakas with their special parts facing outward at the chin, and half-iṣṭakas at the two ends.
One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with large bricks (bṛhatī), and complete the count with half-iṣṭakas.
In the subsequent layer, on the subsequent side, one should place forty-seven foot-bricks (pādeṣṭakā) interlaced.
One [brick] at the chin, six with spikes as their base;
if they are long, one should place four others in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, and two more at the two ends.
The remainder [of the space] is filled with *bṛhatī* verses for the fire-altar.
One should cover [the altar] with eastern bricks and complete the count. 8.
"One should pile the *prauga* on both sides," it is said.

Having made the *prauga* on both sides as large as the fire-altar itself, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, the transverse measurements for the ninth layer are stated as the modifications of the *praugaciti*. 2.
Likewise for the *upadhāna*:

on the next layer, one should place two foot-bricks above the two *cubuka*s; at the two junctions, one should place four long-footed bricks—one long and three others—and four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks in the space [between them], with two *ardhya* bricks at the ends.
One should cover the remaining fire-altar with large bricks (bṛhatī) laid facing east; one should complete the required number with half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā).
Now, there are indeed two kinds of chariot wheels: those with solid hubs and those joined with rims. Since they are indistinguishable [in this context], we consider them to be of one form.

Then he measures out the fire-altar. Having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire-altar—including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*—and having made it a square of equal sides as large as possible within that space, he should have twelve bricks made from the diagonal (*karaṇī*) of that square.
Having laid six of these on the rim, he should divide the remainder into eight parts.
One should lay out another layout in such a way that the corners (sraktayaḥ) fall upon the central squares.
Now, another [method]:
one should have fifteen square bricks made from half a man’s length for the purpose of measurement.
Two hundred and twenty-five of those [bricks], together with the *saratni* and the *prādeśa*, constitute the sevenfold [altar].

(8) Among them, one should insert another sixty-four. With these, he makes it a perfect square. Of that [square], sixteen bricks form the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*). Thirty-three remain; with these, he should enclose the edges on all sides.
(9) The nave consists of sixteen central [bricks]; the sixty-four are the spokes; the altar is the sixty-four; the rim consists of the remaining [bricks]. (10)

One should not draw [the lines] from the center. Having drawn [the lines] around the rim and from within, one should divide the space between the rim and the center into thirty-two parts and remove the sections in reverse order; thus the *āvāpa* (insertion) is removed. 11.
Having divided the rim into sixty-four parts and having drawn them out, one should draw [lines] around the middle; these become one hundred and twenty-eight. 12.
One should divide the spokes into four parts each, and the center into eight parts. 13.

This is the first layout (prastāra). In another layout, one should draw the navel inward at the fourth turn; the rim inward. Having made sixty-four [units] with the rim inward, one should mark them out.
The fivefold division of the spokes is for the two [halves] up to the rim;
there are two spokes in each interval between the rim and the hub, and one spoke in each interval at the hub.
Whatever remains of the hub, that one should divide into eight parts.
This very essence, consisting of sixteen components, is arranged in the pattern of a chariot wheel (20).
"One should pile the mound in the shape of a wooden trough (droṇa)," so it is known.
Now, there are indeed two kinds of troughs: those that are square and those that are circular. Since no distinction is specified, we consider the form of either one of them to be intended.
Then he measures out the fire-altar. Its body is four-cornered. Three *puruṣas* less one-third is its side-measure on the west;
the rear crossbar (*sarū*) is half a *puruṣa* and ten finger-breadths long. One-third less a *puruṣa* is its northward measure.
In this way, it becomes a sevenfold altar provided with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*.

Now follow the modifications of the bricks. Of the *puruṣa* [unit], there are six *ṣaṣṭis*; these same [bricks] are one and a half [units] on one side. Half of them have transverse divisions; they are fourths of the *puruṣa*.

Having laid down six *ṣaṣṭis* in the space between the handle (*tsaru*) and the hip (*śroṇi*), one should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with *bṛhatī* bricks. One should complete the count with half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*).
In the subsequent layer, one should lay down a one-and-a-half brick facing north on the right shoulder; likewise on the left.
In the eastern row, one should place six *ṣaḍbhāgīyā* bricks (9). In the southern and northern [rows], one should place four *caturbhāgīyā* bricks (10).

In front of the *tsaru*, on both sides and above, one should place two *caturbhāgīyā* bricks. Below those two, on both sides, one should place two *adhyardha* bricks extending crosswise (*viṣūcī*). Below those two, in the middle space, one should place two *ṣaṣṭhī* bricks facing east (11).

One should cover the remaining fire-altar with Bṛhatī bricks laid facing east; one should complete the count with half-bricks. Now, another method: by means of sixteen *puruṣas* and twenty hundred [bricks], the sevenfold altar, together with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is accomplished.
Having set aside one of them, he makes the remaining ones circular.

That has been explained previously by the description of the chariot-wheel altar (rathacakracit). Having laid down the sixteenth brick in front and having extended it across, he should trace a circle together with that [sixteenth brick].
That which is cut off from the rear, one should place at the front. 6.
The division of the *pradhīs* is sevenfold. 7.
The widths of the steps are equal to the middle of the *pradhīs*. 8.

One should complete the count of the squares with half-squares. 9. In the subsequent layer, having laid down the middle ring and the rim, one should divide what is below it into two parts. 10. This is the circular Droṇacit altar constructed with nine layers. 11.
The *samūhya* and *paricāyya* are explained by the preceding [section on] the chariot-wheel-altar (*rathacakracit*). 12.
Having caused pits (*cātvāla*) to be dug in the cardinal directions of the *samūhya*, one should collect the earth from them and pile it up. 13.
In the *paricāyya*, there is a difference in the placement of the bricks. 14.
One should enclose it on all sides by circumambulating it to the right.
It is known from scripture: "One should pile the funeral mound.
Having divided the entire fire-altar into fifteen square sections, the manner of laying down the bricks for those sections has been explained.

Having divided a long quadrangle whose width is one and a half parts into three parts, one should mark the two hips from the center of the eastern side-line and remove the two ends. Its division is tenfold;

these [parts] make twenty, and thus the entire fire-altar is completed. In the subsequent arrangement (*prastāra*), one should divide the middle of the *prauga* (fore-part) lengthwise. Its division is sixfold; one should place two of those parts on the two sides.
One should have [the fire-altar] made with a length of three parts and a width of four parts. Of those, there are six transverse divisions of half-bricks;
having placed them at the two ends, one should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with large bricks (*bṛhatī*) laid lengthwise. One should complete the count with half-bricks.
One should increase the height of the fire-altar by a fifth part.

Having divided all that into three parts, one should have bricks made from two parts with the addition of a fourth, a ninth, or a fourteenth part. Having laid down four, nine, or fourteen layers with those [bricks], one should cut off the remainder obliquely toward the downward direction. One should set aside half of it; its constant division is according to the requirements for the reduction or increase of the bricks.
One who desires, "May I conquer the world of Brahman," should pile the fire-altar in the form of a tortoise. It is known:
"There are indeed two kinds of tortoises—those with curved limbs and those that are circular. Since there is no distinction [stated], we consider the shape of either one.
Then he measures out the fire-altar. Its body is square; its side-measure is ten steps. The cutting off of the corners is by two steps each.

In the eastern front, having made four squares measuring one step each, one should cut off their two outer corners diagonally. Likewise on the south, likewise on the west, and likewise on the north. That is the body (ātmā).
The head is five steps long and half a man’s width across. One should cut off its two shoulders by one step each.

If the shoulder (srakti) is cut off, one should raise the foot. Its diagonal measurement is two padas; its length along the side is double that. One should cut off the front shoulder of that [altar] diagonally across two padas. By this, the cutting off of the other feet is explained. On the two rear feet, one should cut off the two rear shoulders.
In this way, the sevenfold altar, together with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed. One should have bricks made for it: fourth-parts of a man, half-parts, and quarter-parts.
One should enclose [the space] with four [sides], each measuring one and a half pādas; by means of a *prakrama*, two feet, and a foot plus a fraction.
One should construct one [side] such that those two [others] may be long and closely joined.
One [side] should be a square of equal sides, measuring half a *dvipada* diagonally.

One should place a square brick at the front of the head-supporting layer. One should place five by five square bricks below the two principal *haṃsa* bricks, and two by two foot-bricks on the feet; thus one should place them on the feet.
Wherever there is a deficiency, one should place half-bricks in that spot.

One should cover the remaining space with fire-bricks (*agni*) consisting of four parts; one should complete the count with half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*). 15. In the subsequent layer, one should place a *haṃsamukhī* brick at the front of the head, with two quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) on either side. 16. Below those two, on both sides, one should place two bricks each, measuring one and a half parts, oriented crosswise (*viṣūcī*), serving as the quarter-bricks. 17.

Below those two, on both sides of the joints, one should place two half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā) [measuring one foot by half a foot]. One should place two two-foot bricks (dvipada) and three three-half-foot bricks (ardheṣṭakā) in each of the foot-spaces (pāda).
Wherever there is a deficiency, one should place half-bricks and foot-bricks in that space.
One should cover the remaining fire-altar with four-part bricks;
one should complete the count with half-bricks. 21.
Now another [method]. 1.
One hundred and twenty *iṣṭakās* of sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśī*) plus a cubit (*aratni*) and a span (*prādeśa*) constitute the sevenfold man.
Having removed five of those sixteen-parts bricks, he arranges the remainder in a circular shape. This is explained by the section on the *droṇaciti*.

Then, with those five sixteen-parts bricks, he should raise the feet toward the intermediate directions and the head toward the east. The method for drawing them around is explained [in the same manner].

The sevenfold division of the *pradhīs* consists of the *pradhi*, the *madhyamā*, and the *prakrama-vyāsas*. Whatever remains in excess should be joined with half-measures of squares. In the subsequent layer (*prastāra*), the division of the feet is like that of the head, and the division of the head is like that of the feet.

One should pile the layers in reverse order as many times as one intends to perform the layerings (prastāra). At the edge of the tortoise-shaped altar, one should place thin loose earth (purīṣa), and in the middle, thick; this same procedure is reversed for the Droṇa altar.
Now, some indeed declare that the Prauga and other altars begin with the Ekavidha.
The teachers say it should be a perfect square. One should have twelve bricks made from its side-measure (*karaṇī*); half of these are for the *ardhya* bricks and half for the *pādya* bricks.
(11) Now, for the fire of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, there is no proportioning by men, nor by *aratni*s or *prādeśa*s.

Or else, it is the standard [fire-altar] tripled. "The fire becomes a threefold praise," and "the fire becomes the twenty-one-fold"—both of these are the Brāhmaṇa explanation; both of these are the Brāhmaṇa explanation. (12–13)
Thus ends the Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra.
